The optimiser wants 0.987, minus 0.438, minus 0.705 and 1.156, and 3.29 dollars of position per dollar of account. Forbidding the shorts keeps 59 per cent of the cut and all of your leverage.

Lesson 72 priced a book in which every position was the same size and left this page the question of how much goes in each. Here is the answer the standard machinery gives, on lesson 71’s four rules over the same twenty-eight moves: 0.987, minus 0.438, minus 0.705 and 1.156. It cuts the standard deviation of the day by 10.65 per cent, which on four positions of two per cent each is 0.78 percentage points of the day. It also asks you to short two of your own four rules and to carry 3.29 dollars of position for every dollar in the account. Forbid the shorts and the answer becomes 0.630 and 0.370 with two rules at zero, which keeps 59 per cent of the cut, holds one dollar of position per dollar of account, and, fitted on twenty-eight days rather than known in advance, delivers a better day than the unconstrained answer does on average.

The inputs are the four rules lesson 71 picked, a 2-bar average against a 5, a 3 against a 10, a 5 against a 20 and an 8 against a 30, over the twenty-eight moves on which every rule in lesson 63’s grid is defined. Their six correlations are lesson 71’s, from 0.6282 to 0.9742. Their standard deviations are close to each other: 0.6375, 0.7218, 0.7265 and 0.7032 in the units the rules return.

Start with the size of the argument. The whole distance from the top row to the bottom is 0.06822, against a starting 0.64074. Everything portfolio construction has to say about this book, from the crudest rule to the exact optimum computed with the answers in hand, is worth 10.65 per cent of the day’s standard deviation. At two per cent a position and lesson 71’s average correlation of 0.7887 for these four, equal weights make the day 7.339 per cent and the optimum makes it 6.557 per cent. The whole prize is eight tenths of a percentage point a day. It is worth having and it is not worth a great deal of trouble, and knowing which of those it is before you start is most of what this page is for.

Read the second row next, because it is the one people actually run. Inverse variance collects 0.89 per cent of the available 10.65, which is a twelfth. It fails because the four standard deviations are nearly the same, so weighting by them barely moves anything, and the whole of the prize on this book lives in the correlations. A weighting that ignores correlations on a set of rules whose correlations run from 0.63 to 0.97 is solving a problem this book does not have.

Then the two that matter. The unconstrained answer takes another 4.33 percentage points off the day, moving the cut from 6.32 per cent to 10.65, and it buys that with two short legs totalling 1.143 and a gross position of 3.287 dollars for every dollar of account. The constraint costs two fifths of the prize and removes all of the leverage.

Module 9’s card gains a third column, and it is the weight this page gives each rule, written twice: once as the optimiser returns it and once with the shorts forbidden. Lesson 75 is where the whole card gets spent at once.
What twenty-eight days can pay for

The weights above came out of ten numbers — four variances and six covariances — estimated from twenty-eight observations. That is not obviously too few, and it is not obviously enough, so measure it rather than arguing about it.

Treat the covariance measured above as if it were the truth. Draw T observations from it, fit the optimiser to the draw as though that were all you had, then score the resulting weights against the truth you started from. The gap between the score and the true optimum is the estimation error, and it is the only thing this experiment contains. Twenty thousand draws at each T, from seed 20260905, so the third column is steady to a tenth of a point and the fourth to two tenths.

The first row is the honest verdict on the weights this page opened with. Fitted on twenty-eight observations, the unconstrained optimiser delivers 0.60798 rather than the 0.57252 it prints, which is 48.0 per cent of the prize rather than all of it. It still beats equal weights, and comfortably: on this book the optimiser is not a mistake and the folk claim that dividing by N always wins is not what the arithmetic says.

The fourth column is the finding, and it has to be read against the second. Fitted on twenty-eight observations, the unconstrained answer beats the constrained one on 50.4 per cent of draws, which is a coin flip, while delivering 0.60798 on average against the 0.60021 the constraint delivers with no estimation at all. The weights you cannot hold win half the time, lose on average, and carry three dollars of position for every one either way. It takes sixty observations before the unconstrained answer wins five times in six and 125 before it wins essentially always, and 125 daily observations is six months of closes.

Now look at the weights themselves rather than at what they deliver. Resample the twenty-eight days with replacement four thousand times from seed 20260906, refit, and read the middle ninety of a hundred results:
2-and-5, fitted at 0.987: lands between 0.724 and 1.316.
3-and-10, fitted at minus 0.438: lands between minus 0.881 and minus 0.043.
5-and-20, fitted at minus 0.705: lands between minus 1.381 and 0.081, and is positive in 6.6 per cent of resamples.
Gross position, fitted at 3.287: median 3.194, and above three dollars per dollar of account in 63.9 per cent of resamples.

The standard deviation those weights deliver is stable. The weights are not. A weight of minus 0.705 whose own resamples run from minus 1.381 to plus 0.081 is not a decision about a rule, it is the residue of ten estimates fighting over twenty-eight days, and printing it to three figures is the part that misleads. And 153 of the four thousand resamples produced a covariance matrix with no inverse at all, so on nearly one draw in twenty-five of your own days the method does not return a wrong answer, it returns none.

Which is where the constraint earns its keep, and it does more than protect you from leverage. Forbidding negative weights is arithmetically close to admitting the covariance is measured badly and pulling it toward something simpler: shrink this book’s covariance halfway toward the single average correlation lesson 72 used and the optimiser returns a gross position of 1.205 and a standard deviation of 0.59512, against the constraint’s 1.000 and 0.60021. Two different admissions of the same ignorance, arriving within one per cent of each other on the day and a fifth of a dollar on the position.
So run the optimiser with the shorts forbidden, and take the 6.32 per cent it can hold over the 10.65 it cannot.

That the 10.65 per cent is free. Gross position goes from one dollar to 3.287, and every cost that scales with what you trade scales with that: lesson 12’s spread on the way in and out, lesson 59’s impact on the way in, lesson 68’s capacity on the size you can hold at all. The objective contains none of them, so it will happily buy eight tenths of a percentage point of daily standard deviation with a tripling of the bill. On the fund in lesson 12 that trade is obviously worth it and on the micro cap it is obviously not, and the formula cannot tell them apart because it was never shown the quotes.

That the simulation measures the whole error. It does not, and it flatters the optimiser by construction. The truth it draws from is the same covariance the twenty-eight days produced, so what the table prices is estimation error and nothing else. It says nothing about the covariance being wrong in the first place, which is the larger problem and the next page’s.

That four rules is the hard case. It is the easy one. Ten parameters from twenty-eight observations is uncomfortable; twenty rules is 210 parameters from the same twenty-eight days, and at twenty-eight rules the measured matrix stops having an inverse at all, so the optimiser does not return a bad answer, it fails to return one. The number of parameters grows as the square of the number of rules and the data does not, which is why every professional treatment of this problem is about shrinking, constraining or factoring the matrix rather than inverting what you measured.

And the concession that costs most: this page treated the covariance as one object measured on one window, and it is not one object. Split the same twenty-eight moves in half and the average correlation between the four rules is 0.5673 in the first fourteen and 0.9247 in the last fourteen, and the weights fitted on the first half are 0.308, 0.225, minus 0.731 and 1.197 rather than 0.987, minus 0.438, minus 0.705 and 1.156. In the last fourteen it is worse than unstable: three of the four rules hold the same position on every one of those days, their correlations are exactly one, and the covariance matrix has no inverse at all. Lesson 74 starts there, with the half of your own data on which the machinery on this page does not run.

Compute the standard deviation of your book at equal weights and at the unconstrained optimum, and take the ratio. Ten minutes, and you end holding one number, the most that reweighting can ever do for you, which you compare against the 10.65 per cent on this page and against what your costs would rise by at the optimum’s gross position.
The cost that scales with the 3.29 dollars of position the optimiser asks for.
